persons.note: A CONTEMPORARY CHICAGO PAPER OF 1833-1835 PRINTS THIS PERSON BY NAME IN THE TOWN. Read from newspaper_1833_1835. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G1b), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. newspaper_1833_1835 names this person at Chicago by 1 July 1835 and nothing says when they came. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the person was at Chicago by 1 July 1835 on this record's own evidence. No figure is drawn (L1).

merge_ruling.for_merge: The initial L agrees with Liman and both cards are Chicago readings of the summer of 1835.
merge_ruling.against_merge: ONE ISSUE SETS BOTH SPELLINGS IN TWO DIFFERENT COLUMNS, WHICH IS EVIDENCE AGAINST AND NOT FOR. The Democrat of 1 July 1835 prints 'Curtis, Liman' in the post-office return at column 4 and 'L. Curtiss' at column 13 of the same issue. A compositor who set Curtis in one column and Curtiss in another that day was distinguishing two names, not wavering over one; C9 asks for a printing caught setting both spellings FOR ONE MAN and this is a printing caught keeping them apart. L. G. Curtiss is besides set 'L. G. Curtiss' on 22 July and 'Curtiss, L. G.' on 5 August 1835, three settings that never drop the second s, and the town holds curtiss_j beside him. The middle initial G is printed on the Curtiss side and absent on Liman's. D7.

age_band.note: AN AGE BAND, NEVER A YEAR. No source this project holds bears on when this person was born, so the band is drawn from the only committed sex by age distribution the project has - the 1840 Chicago schedule, five years after the scene and a town twice the size - seeded by this person's own id ('curtiss_l_g:age_bands_1840'). AND THE CONDITIONING IS THE MODEL'S, NOT A SOURCE'S: that a roll naming a person in their own right names somebody 15 or over. The 1840 schedule counts a child as a tally inside a household and never as a correspondent; 15 rather than 20 because an apprentice or a journeyman stands on a trade roll. No source states this rule. No exact year is written, because a year drawn from a decadal band would read as a record of a birth.
